Aesthetic value resists any coherent reduction to purely subjective preference or individual psychological response because the very structure of our encounters with beauty and art points beyond the confines of personal taste. In the phenomenology of genuine aesthetic experience, when we judge a work to be beautiful we do not merely report an internal feeling but implicitly issue a call to others to share in that judgment, asserting a kind of intersubjective validity that carries normative weight. This dimension reveals itself in the way aesthetic pleasure feels as if it demands agreement, as though the object's qualities themselves solicit a response that transcends the idiosyncrasies of any single mind, a feature that cannot be captured by frameworks that treat beauty as nothing more than private sensation or conditioned reaction.
The practice of aesthetic criticism further exposes the inadequacy of subjectivism, for it operates through an elaborate apparatus of reasons, standards, and education that treats aesthetic assessments as answerable to considerations extending well beyond any individual's immediate response. Critics offer arguments grounded in formal properties, historical context, technical mastery, and cultural resonance, presupposing that some judgments are more perceptive, informed, or refined than others and that cultivation through attentive study can improve one's capacity to discern value. Education in the arts is predicated on the idea that novices can be guided toward more adequate appreciations, implying a hierarchy of insight rather than a flat landscape of equally valid personal preferences, and this entire critical enterprise would collapse into incoherence if aesthetic value were reducible solely to whatever happens to strike each person at a given moment.
Finally, any attempt to embrace aesthetic relativism as a thoroughgoing alternative founders on an internal regress that erodes its own normative standing. If every preference is held to be equally valid with no external standard by which to adjudicate among them, then the very preference for relativism or pluralism over more dogmatic or universalist approaches becomes nothing more than one subjective inclination among others, lacking any special authority to command assent or to criticize opposing views. This self-undermining dynamic leaves relativism without resources to sustain its own position as a coherent doctrine, revealing once again that aesthetic value cannot be coherently confined to the realm of individual psychology without draining it of the normative and intersubjective dimensions that define our actual engagement with art and beauty.
--- END ---
